### PREFACE


viii

As we launch the eleventh edition of Pathologic Basis of Disease , it is

worth pausing for a moment to consider the future of pathology as a

discipline and the role of this textbook in the education of twenty-first

century students. It is apparent that an understanding of disease

mechanisms is based more than ever on a strong foundation of basic

science. In turn, new insights have spawned an ever-increasing num -

ber of “targeted therapies” geared to treat disease more effectively and

precisely than in the past. Full understanding of the rationale for these

therapies requires a firm grounding in disease pathophysiology and

relevant basic cellular and molecular biology. To ensure readers have

the necessary knowledge, we have retained and updated our introduc-

tory chapter titled, “The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease, ” and have

woven fundamental aspects of cellular and molecular biology into

discussion of disease throughout this edition.

In the preface of the first edition (1957), Stanley Robbins wrote

“The pathologist is interested not only in the recognition of structural

alterations, but also in their significance, i.e., the effects of these changes

on cellular and tissue function and ultimately the effect of these changes

on the patient. It is not a discipline isolated from the living patient, but

rather a basic approach to a better understanding of disease and there -

fore a foundation of sound clinical medicine.” Here, we have endeavored

to continue to illustrate the principles of pathology that Dr. Robbins

enunciated with such elegance and clarity over half a century ago.

This edition, like all its predecessors, has been extensively revised,

and some areas have been completely rewritten. A few examples of


### significant changes are as follows:


• C hapter 2 has been updated to include novel pathways of cell death

beyond the long-established pathways of necrosis and apoptosis.

Indeed, the distinction between these two is being blurred. Au -

tophagy, which has begun to take center stage in diseases ranging

from aging to cancer and neurodegeneration, has been revised, as

have the possible molecular mechanisms of aging.

• C hapter 4 has updated information on coagulation pathways, and

current knowledge of sepsis and septic shock

• C hapter 11 includes a discussion of the pathophysiology of heart

failure with preserved ejection fraction.

• C hapter 5 (Genetics) includes new discussions of diseases caused

by genetic mosaicism as well as Rett syndrome, a disease of epigen-

etic misprogramming, as well as new approaches to diagnosis, such

as liquid biopsies.

• C hapter 6 (Immunity) includes an extensively revised and updated

discussion of amyloidosis.

• C hapter 7 (Cancer) is updated to cover changes in our understand -

ing of cancer pathogenesis and new approaches to molecular diag-

nostics.

• C hapters 8 (Infectious Disease) and 15 (Lung) have updated dis -

cussions of SARS-CoV-2 and COVID-19.

• C hapter 9 (Environmental Diseases) has expanded coverage of the

role health care disparities play in explaining variation in the inci-

dence and severity of various diseases across different communities

and an updated discussion of obesity, informed by the remarkably

efficacy of GLP-1 agonists.

• C hapter 11 (Blood Vessels) includes a discussion of the patho -

physiology of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.

• C hapter 18 (Liver) contains updates on the nomenclature, diagnos -

tic criteria, and pathogenesis of metabolic dysfunction2associated

steatotic liver disease (MASLD), which continues to increase in

prevalence at an alarming rate in high-resource countries.

• C hapter 20 (Kidney) has a new discussion of podocytopathies,

particularly minimal change disease, now known to be caused by

autoantibodies against slit diaphragm proteins.

• C hapter 23 (Breast) has been reorganized to help students better

understand the pathobiology of breast cancer.

• C hapter 25 (Skin) includes new images demonstrating variation in

the appearance of skin diseases among patients with lighter or

darker skin coloration, alleviating an oversight of previous editions.

• C hapter 28 (Central Nervous System) has new information about

the pathogenesis of demyelinating and neurodegenerative diseases

and a completely revised classification of brain tumors based on

molecular genetics and morphology, as recommended by interna -

tional committees.

• C hapter 29 (Eye) has an update on the pathogenesis of age-related

macular degeneration, supported by superb new figures.

• C hapters 5, 9, 15, 19, 20, 22, 23, 24, and 27, covering genetic dis -

eases, environmental diseases, and diseases of the lung, pancreas,

kidney, female genital tract and placenta, breast, endocrine system,

and peripheral nerves and muscle, respectively, all have a fresh look

brought in by new contributors.

• I n addition to the revision and reorganization of the text, many new

photographs and schematic diagrams have been added or revised.

We made the changes highlighted above while remaining focused

on the same longstanding overarching goals, which serve as our guid -


### ing principles:


• T o integrate into the discussion of pathologic processes and disor -

ders the newest established information available—morphologic as

well as molecular.

• T o organize information into logical and uniform presentations,

facilitating readability, comprehension, and learning.

• T o maintain the book at a reasonable size and yet provide adequate

discussion of significant lesions, processes, and disorders. Indeed,

despite the addition of new information, the overall length of the

book has decreased by approximately 100 pages. One of our most

challenging tasks is to decide what to eliminate to make room for

key new findings.

• T o place great emphasis on clarity of writing and proper use of

language in the recognition that struggling to comprehend is time-

consuming and wearisome and gets in the way of the learning

process.

• T o make this text useful to students throughout all their years in

medical school and into their residencies—but, at the same time, to

provide sufficient detail and depth to meet the needs of more ad -

vanced readers.

We have repeatedly been told by readers that up-to-datedness is a

special feature that makes this book very valuable. We have strived to

remain current by providing new information from the recent litera -

ture, up to the current year, and by adding coverage of the COVID-19

epidemic.

We now live in a digital age, so an eBook is available to those who

own the print version. Such access gives the reader the ability to search

across the entire text, bookmark passages, add personal notes, use

### ACKNOWLEDGMENTS


x

First and foremost, all five of us offer thanks to our contributing

authors for their commitment to this textbook. Many are veterans

of previous editions; others are new to the eleventh edition. All are

acknowledged in the table of contents. Their names lend authority to

this book, for which we are grateful. As in previous editions, the five of

us have chosen not to add our own names to the chapters we have been

responsible for writing, in part or whole.

Several colleagues have enhanced the text by reading various chap-

ters and providing helpful critiques in their area of expertise, including

Dr. Vaishali Sanchorawala, Boston University, and Sandro Santagata,

Brigham and Women’s Hospital. Many colleagues provided photo -

graphic gems from their collections. They are individually acknowl -

edged in the text.

Many individuals associated with our publisher, Elsevier, deserve

our sincerest thanks. Jeremy Bowes, our publisher, has been highly

supportive throughout the planning and work on this edition. A spe -

cial note of thanks goes to our past Director of Content Development,

Rebecca Gruliow, who has been a partner for almost two decades until

her much-deserved retirement. We are enjoying our partnership with

“Becca’s” outstanding replacement, Kevin Travers, and have benefitted

from the marvelous efforts of Carrie Stetz, our Production Manager.

Undoubtedly there are many others who may have been left out unwit-

tingly—to them, we say “thank you” and apologies for not recognizing

you individually. We also want to acknowledge many readers—

students, residents, and faculty members—scattered around the globe

whose comments improve the book. We are impressed by their careful

reading of the text.

Efforts of this magnitude take a toll on the families of the authors.

We thank our spouses, Raminder Kumar, Ann Abbas, Erin Malone,

Runi Chattopadhyay, and Kankana Roy, for their patience, love, and

support of this venture, and for their tolerance of our absences.

Jon C. Aster
